chapter_title_en: Face to Face With the Spirit-Blight
chapter_seo_title: Dao-Twisted World Chapter 478: Li Huowang Faces the Invisible Spirit-Blight
chapter_meta_description: Li Huowang confronts his first Spirit-Blight—a possessed, sadistic Nine-Colored Deer that feeds on twilight and is invisible to any mortal carrying the Ten Emotions. Zhuge Yuan’s darkest secret comes to light.
og_title: The Spirit-Blight That Feeds on Sunset
og_description: A possessed deer that enjoys torture. A monster no living human can see. Li Huowang’s only option is to set himself on fire.
twitter_title: Face to Face With Karma’s Flesh: The Spirit-Blight
twitter_description: Zhuge Yuan once had to kill his own possessed friend. Now Li Huowang faces the same kind of monster—and he can’t even see it.

lore_anchors.definition: A being born from incarnate karmic sin; it possesses hosts and delights in slow, sadistic cruelty. The name emphasizes “Blight” (孽) over “Spirit”—the possession itself is the weapon.
A divine guardian from the *Classic of Mountains and Seas*, depicted here as a rotting six-legged doe called the Nine-Colored Deer. Its mythological majesty has been corrupted into a horror.
A twisted expansion of the Buddhist Eight Sufferings. In the Dao-Twisted World, any living human carrying these cannot perceive a Spirit-Blight’s true form.

Straw effigies used in ancient Chinese sacrifice, then discarded. The *Dao De Jing* quote “Heaven and earth treat all things as straw dogs” implies cosmic indifference; in the Dao-Twisted World, it hints at active malice.
A Daoist exorcism sword made from coins strung on red cord. Traditionally used for fengshui and spirit-banishing, here it damages the Spirit-Blight but cannot kill it.
A mahjong tile used by Li Huowang as a distraction; the Red Center is one of the four directional tiles in a standard set.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Why can’t Li Huowang see the real Spirit-Blight?
cultural_notes_faq.a: Because every living person carries the Ten Emotions and Eight Sufferings—a karmic filter that blinds mortals to the entity’s true location. Only the shell (the deer) is visible.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Is the Nine-Colored Deer from real Chinese mythology?
cultural_notes_faq.a: Yes—Yingzhao (英招) appears in the *Classic of Mountains and Seas*. It was originally a divine guardian, not a sadistic monster. The novel deliberately corrupts the original myth.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Why does the Spirit-Blight torture the rat instead of just eating it?
cultural_notes_faq.a: Because Spirit-Blights are defined by “孽” (karmic sin), not by hunger. Their purpose is cruelty itself—the suffering is the point, not the meal.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Will the Bronze Coin Sword work against the Spirit-Blight?
cultural_notes_faq.a: It deals damage (black smoke, withering flesh), but not a killing blow. The sword is effective against common spirits but outmatched here. Li Huowang will need a stronger strategy.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Why does Li Huowang take off his robe and strike a fire striker on himself at the end?
cultural_notes_faq.a: That is a deliberate cliffhanger. Given the chapter’s trajectory, he is preparing either a self-sacrificial move, a distraction tactic, or a way to channel yang fire against a yin entity.
